subtopicTitle: De Moivre's theorem — statement, proof, applications

cards.back: If $z=r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)$ with $r>0$ and $\theta\in\mathbb{R}$, then for any integer $n\geq0$, $z^n=r^n(\cos(n\theta)+i\sin(n\theta))$.

cards.front: Prove De Moivre's theorem by induction on $n$.
cards.back: Base ($n=0$): $z^0=1=r^0(\cos0+i\sin0)$. Assume true for $k$: $z^k=r^k(\cos(k\theta)+i\sin(k\theta))$. Then $z^{k+1}=z^k\cdot z=r^{k+1}(\cos((k+1)\theta)+i\sin((k+1)\theta))$ by angle-addition formulas. Holds for all $n\geq0$.

cards.front: Use De Moivre to compute $(1+i)^4$ in rectangular form.
How does De Moivre yield the multiple-angle formula for $\cos n\theta$?
cards.back: Expand $[\cos\theta+i\sin\theta]^n$ via binomial theorem; equate real part to $\cos n\theta$.

cards.front: State the formula for the $n$th roots of $re^{i\theta}$ using De Moivre.
